NOT REFUTED. I fetched Cole's text twice, by two routes, rather than trust a verifier on a famous opening. The Project Gutenberg file 46333 states its own provenance: 'Title: The social contract & discourses. Author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Translator: G. D. H. Cole', from page images supplied by the Google Books Library Project, and the title page inside reads 'London & Toronto, Published by J. M. Dent & Sons, In New York by E. P. Dutton & Co, Everyman's Library, Edited by Ernest Rhys, Philosophy and Theology, ROUSSEAU'S SOCIAL CONTRACT, ETC., Translated with Introduction by G.D.H. Cole, Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford'. The structure runs FOREWORD, then BOOK I with its untitled preamble ('I mean to inquire if, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration'), then CHAPTER I, then the chapter title SUBJECT OF THE FIRST BOOK, and then, as the first words of the chapter: 'Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains. One thinks himself the master of others, and still remains a greater slave than they.'

THE PUNCTUATION IS THE WHOLE TEST HERE, AND IT PASSES. The semicolon after free is Cole's own, printed in this text, not a modernisation and not somebody's tidying; Cole also keeps the lower-case m on 'man' in the body of the sentence while the drop capital raises the first letter, which is how the proposal has it. The comma-spliced modern rendering 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' is the one that would have been wrong for Cole, and it is not what was proposed.

THE LOCATOR IS EXACT, AND ITS ONE AMBIGUITY IS HANDLED. The source says 'Book I, chapter 1, the opening sentence', which is precisely right: Book I opens with a short untitled preamble of three paragraphs before Chapter I, so the sentence opens the chapter and not the book, and the source line says chapter, not book. If it had said 'the opening sentence of The Social Contract' I would have refuted it.

THE DATE. Cole's Everyman translation is standardly dated 1913, and the text corroborates it from inside: Cole's own introduction says Rousseau's name is a controversial watchword 'a hundred and fifty years after the publication of the Social Contract', which was published in 1762. 1913 stands.

EVERY OTHER TEST. shipped.js on the exact wording with 'Jean-Jacques Rousseau': shipped [], near [], yearCount 0, not at cap, not banned. Rousseau is unused in the year and appears once in the month's verdict directory, so nobody is doubled. Scope is clear: 1762, translation 1913, so not scripture, not film, not lyric, not proverb, not business, not oratory, nothing after 1999. Rousseau writes in his own voice, so there is no speaker to name. Nothing needs a content warning; the chains are a figure for political subjection, with no description of anything a reader would need warning of. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work. The quotation ends in a full stop, carries no quotation marks, is prose and is kept as prose. The source line leads with the author's name, carries no dash, and is 112 characters.

THE ONE OBJECTION WORTH STATING AND THEN ANSWERING. Rule 3 bars famous and bleak. This line is famous and it names a hard fact, but it is not bleak: it is the first move of an argument that legitimate authority is possible, and Rousseau says so in the next breath, 'What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.' Read at six in the morning in a month about what is owed, it is a demand rather than a defeat. Ship it.
